verdict: Caution on Nagpur logistics & warehousing: lend only to fire-compliant, diversified 3PL operators with clean title and verified insurance; avoid single-client godown owners in encroached clusters.
title: Nagpur Logistics & Warehousing: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Nagpur godown is a shed that rents space and moves cartons; cash comes from occupancy and throughput, not from the building.** The operator takes rent per square foot plus handling charges, pays for land, construction, power, security and labour, and collects from a handful of large consignors. Value sits in location (Wardhaman Nagar, the MIDC belts) and in the tenancy book; cash sits in receivables from 3PL clients and in the stock the client stores. **Capex is heavy and lumpy, working capital is short but collection-driven, and pricing power is thin because a shed is a commodity.**

## What has changed now
**Two fires in Nagpur in the same week — seven godowns gutted with Rs 4.81 crore of goods destroyed, and a plastic packaging warehouse in Wardhaman Nagar — and firefighting was hampered by encroachments [1][2][3].** That is local news, dated 31 October 2026, and it is the single most important fact for us this month. **The loss falls first on the stored goods, then on the shed owner's rent and reputation; encroached access means insurers and fire brigades will push back.** Peer results are strong but national, not Nagpur: Delhivery crossed Rs 3,000 crore quarterly revenue with 19.8% growth [4][5][6], and VRL saw 18% revenue growth with 21.8% EBITDA margin [7]. **Do not read national parcel growth as Nagpur shed demand.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue 3PL and e-commerce fulfilment operators with multi-client books, and industrial tenants tied to Nagpur's MIDC manufacturing.** Rating evidence shows the model works when diversified: one warehousing player runs interest coverage of 11 times with margins over 24% [8][9], another holds gearing of 0.22x with Rs 72.08 crore of liquid funds [10]. **Avoid single-consignor godowns, plastic and packaging storage in dense clusters, and sheds on encroached land [1][2].**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the shed, not the story: mortgage the land, take rent receivables escrow, and insist on a fire-compliant, insured asset.** When a proposal lands, check the fire NOC, the insurance policy schedule and the access road width; if the shed sits in an encroached lane, ask for the municipal layout approval before sanctioning [1]. **Take monthly rent-roll, occupancy, receivables ageing and insurance-renewal proof every month.** Watch the working-capital cycle: one peer's cycle stretched from 39 days in FY23 to 77 days in FY24 as collection days moved from 52 to 82 [11], so if receivables cross that pattern, ask for the top-five debtor list and stop enhancing limits.

## Early-warning signs
**Rent arrears from anchor tenants, insurance lapse, a fire or encroachment notice, and occupancy falling below the sanctioned base are the triggers.** Collect from customer the current rent roll, occupancy percentage and insurance cover value — the sources give us none of these for Nagpur. **Where sources say little about this city, lean on first principles and the peer numbers above.**
watch: occupancy falls below sanctioned base -> freeze limit enhancement and re-price
Insurance renewal and fire NOC (annual, verify monthly)
lapsed policy or missing NOC -> stop disbursement until cured
Receivables ageing and top-five debtor list (monthly)
collection days stretch past 82 -> ask for debtor list and cap exposure [11]
Fire or encroachment notice from municipality (event-based)
notice received -> inspect site and reassess collateral [1]
arrears beyond one cycle -> move to Caution and seek escrow top-up
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
